outcomes.text: Define movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition as the seven characteristics of living organisms.
Compare plant, animal and bacterial cell structures; identify and explain their functions, cell division, specialised cells, and levels of organisation.
Use magnification = image size ÷ actual size, calculate specimen magnification or size, and convert millimetres to micrometres.

topics.title: B3 Movement into and out of cells

outcomes.text: Explain diffusion and its cellular importance, and investigate how surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance affect its rate.
Explain osmosis and water movement through cell membranes; investigate concentration effects and relate water potential to turgor, plasmolysis and organism water balance.
Explain active transport against a concentration gradient using respiratory energy, including its importance in molecular movement and root ion uptake.
Identify elements in carbohydrates, fats and proteins; describe their component molecules and perform tests for starch, reducing sugars, proteins and fats.
Describe enzymes as protein catalysts, explain specificity and action, and investigate how temperature and pH affect activity through collisions, shape and denaturation.
Explain photosynthesis, its word and balanced equations, chlorophyll’s role, carbohydrate uses, mineral requirements, and effects of light, carbon dioxide and temperature.
Relate leaf surface area, thinness and named structures to adaptations enabling efficient photosynthesis.
Describe a balanced diet, sources and functions of nutrients, and vitamin-deficiency diseases scurvy and rickets.
Identify digestive organs and explain ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion in relation to their functions.
Distinguish physical and chemical digestion; explain enzyme, hydrochloric acid and bile functions, including secretion sites and fat emulsification.
State xylem and phloem functions and identify their positions in roots, stems and leaves of non-woody dicotyledonous plants.
Identify root hair cells, explain their large surface area, and describe water’s pathway from roots through xylem to mesophyll.
Explain transpiration and water-vapour movement, investigate environmental effects on its rate, and explain wilting.
Describe phloem translocation of sucrose and amino acids from sources, which release them, to sinks, which use or store them.
Describe vessel-based circulatory systems with pumps and valves, including fish single circulation, mammal double circulation and its advantages.
Identify heart structures and explain blood flow, heart function, monitoring methods, exercise effects, coronary heart disease risks and prevention.
Describe artery, vein and capillary structures, including wall thickness, lumen diameter and valves in veins.
List red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma as the components of blood.
Describe a pathogen as an organism that causes disease.
Identify the principal breathing-system structures, including lungs, airways, diaphragm, ribs, muscles, alveoli and capillaries.
State energy uses including muscle contraction, synthesis, division, growth, nerve impulses and temperature maintenance.
State that electrical impulses travel along neurones.
Describe hormones as blood-transported glandular chemicals affecting specific target organs.
Define homeostasis as maintaining a constant internal environment.
Define a drug as a substance that changes chemical reactions in the body.
Describe asexual reproduction as producing genetically identical offspring from one parent.
Describe sexual reproduction as gamete fusion producing genetically varied offspring.
Identify and draw the listed structures of insect-pollinated flowers.
Identify male reproductive structures and state their functions.
Define an STI as an infection transmitted through sexual contact.
State that DNA-containing chromosomes carry genetic information in genes.
Describe mitosis as nuclear division producing genetically identical cells.
Understand inheritance, genotypes, phenotypes, homozygous and heterozygous conditions, dominant and recessive alleles, pedigrees, genetic diagrams, phenotypic ratios and Punnett squares.
Understand variation, continuous and discontinuous phenotypes, mutation, and mutation’s role in producing new alleles.
Explain natural selection, antibiotic resistance, selective breeding, and artificial selection over generations to improve crops and domesticated animals.
Understand the Sun as the principal energy source and describe energy transfer through organisms into the environment.
Construct and interpret food chains and webs; identify producers, consumers, trophic levels and decomposers; explain energy losses and human impacts.
Describe carbon cycling through photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, fossil-fuel formation and combustion.
Understand ecosystems and biodiversity, causes of habitat destruction, and deforestation’s effects including extinction, soil loss, flooding and increased atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Explain causes of endangerment or extinction and describe conservation through protection, education, captive breeding and seed banks.
Describe particle structures and properties of solids, liquids and gases; explain state changes and temperature- or pressure-dependent gas volumes.
Explain diffusion using kinetic particle theory and relate gas diffusion rates to relative molecular masses.
Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures.

subtopics.title: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Describe atomic structure, particle charges and masses, proton and mass numbers, electronic configurations, and relationships between groups, periods and electrons.
Define isotopes, interpret atomic and ionic symbols, and explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
Describe ion formation, ionic bonding, ionic lattices and ionic compound properties, using dot-and-cross diagrams where required.
Describe covalent bonding in specified molecules and relate simple molecular structures and bonding to their physical and electrical properties.
Describe graphite and diamond structures and relate their bonding and properties to specified uses.
Describe metallic bonding and explain metals’ electrical conductivity and malleability using their structure and bonding.
State formulas, define molecular formulas, deduce formulas, construct and balance word and symbol equations, and include state symbols or ionic equations.
Define relative atomic and molecular or formula masses and calculate reacting masses using simple proportions without moles.
Use concentration units, the mole and Avogadro constant, molar relationships, molar gas volume and stoichiometry calculations including limiting reactants.
Explain electrolysis, identify cell components and electrode charges, describe products and observations, track charge transfer, and construct cathode half-equations.
Explain how hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells generate electricity with water as the only product, including their advantages and disadvantages compared with petrol engines.
Distinguish exothermic and endothermic reactions, interpret and construct pathway diagrams, define enthalpy change and activation energy, and relate bond changes to energy.
Identify physical and chemical changes and explain the differences between them.
Explain how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts affect reaction rates using collision theory; investigate and interpret rate data.
Define redox, oxidation and reduction using oxygen transfer, electron transfer and oxidation numbers, and identify these processes in reactions.
Describe acid, base and alkali reactions, indicator effects, pH comparisons and neutralisation producing salt and water.
Classify acidic, basic and amphoteric oxides, and describe amphoteric reactions with acids and bases.
Prepare, separate and purify soluble salts, define hydrated and anhydrous substances, and prepare insoluble salts by precipitation.
Describe Periodic Table organisation, metallic trends across periods, group similarities from electronic structure, and trends within groups.
Describe Group I metals and their trends in melting point, density and water reactivity, and predict properties of other Group I elements.
Describe Group VII halogens, their appearances and trends, explain halogen displacement reactions, and predict properties of other group members.
Describe transition elements as dense, high-melting metals that form coloured compounds and frequently act as catalysts.
Describe noble gases as unreactive, monatomic gases and explain their low reactivity using electronic configuration.
Compare metals and non-metals’ physical properties and describe metals’ reactions with dilute acids, cold water and steam.
Relate aluminium and copper uses to their low density, conductivity and corrosion resistance.
Describe alloy composition, examples, properties and uses; identify alloy structures and explain their greater hardness and strength.
Use the reactivity series to describe metal reactions, explain displacement and acid or water reactions, and deduce reactivity from results.
State rusting conditions, describe barrier methods and galvanising, and explain sacrificial protection using reactivity and electron loss.
Relate extraction difficulty to reactivity, describe iron extraction from hematite in the blast furnace, and state aluminium’s ore and extraction method.
Test for water and purity, explain distilled water’s laboratory use, and describe domestic water treatment by sedimentation, filtration, carbon and chlorination.
State clean-air composition and identify sources of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, particulates, methane, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide.
Explain how planting trees, reducing livestock farming and fossil-fuel use, and expanding hydrogen and renewable energy can limit climate change.
Explain how low-sulfur fuels and calcium-oxide flue-gas desulfurisation reduce acid rain.
Explain greenhouse warming through thermal-energy absorption, reflection and emission, including reduced energy loss to space.
Explain nitrogen-oxide formation in car engines and catalytic-converter removal using 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
Draw and interpret displayed molecular formulas showing every atom and bond.
State that saturated compounds contain only single carbon–carbon bonds.
State that unsaturated compounds contain at least one non-single carbon–carbon bond.
Define a homologous series as similar compounds with similar chemical properties.
Describe homologous series as sharing a general formula and showing trends in physical properties.
Name and draw displayed formulas for methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol.
Identify compound types from names ending in -ane, -ene or -ol, or from formulas.
Name and draw structural and displayed formulas for unbranched alkanes and alkenes with up to four carbon atoms.
Name coal, natural gas and petroleum as fossil fuels.
State that methane is the main constituent of natural gas.
Define hydrocarbons as compounds containing only hydrogen and carbon.
State that petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
Describe separating petroleum into useful fractions by fractional distillation.
State the uses of refinery gas, gasoline, naphtha, diesel oil and bitumen fractions.
Describe how fraction properties change upward in the column: shorter chains and lower boiling points.
State that alkanes have single covalent bonds and are saturated hydrocarbons.
Describe alkanes as generally unreactive except in combustion.
State that alkenes contain carbon–carbon double bonds and are unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Describe using aqueous bromine to distinguish saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Describe cracking larger alkanes at high temperature with a catalyst to produce alkenes and hydrogen.
Describe alkene addition reactions with bromine, hydrogen using nickel, and steam using an acid catalyst.
Describe the complete combustion of ethanol.
State that ethanol is used as a solvent and fuel.
Define polymers as large molecules made from many smaller monomers.
Describe poly(ethene) formation by addition polymerisation of ethene.
Identify repeat units in addition and condensation polymers.
Deduce an addition polymer repeat unit from an alkene, and the alkene from its repeat unit.
Describe differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Describe and draw nylon as a polyamide.

topics.title: C12 Experimental techniques and chemical analysis

outcomes.text: Name suitable apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume.
Define solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue and filtrate.
Describe an acid–base titration using a burette, volumetric pipette and suitable indicator.
Explain how an indicator identifies a titration end-point.
Describe paper chromatography for separating soluble coloured mixtures using a suitable solvent.
Interpret chromatograms to identify unknowns by comparison and distinguish pure from impure substances.
State and use Rf = distance travelled by substance ÷ distance travelled by solvent.
Describe and explain separation or purification using solvents, filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable separation and purification methods from information about the substances.

subtopics.title: Purity from melting and boiling points

outcomes.text: Identify substances and assess purity using melting-point and boiling-point data.

topics.title: C12.5 Identification of ions and gases

outcomes.text: Describe tests for carbonate, halide, nitrate and sulfate anions.
Describe sodium-hydroxide and ammonia tests for ammonium, calcium, copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) and zinc ions.
Describe tests for ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen and oxygen gases.
Use flame tests to identify lithium, sodium, potassium and copper(II) cations.

topics.title: P1.1 Physical quantities and measurement techniques

outcomes.text: Describe using rulers and measuring cylinders to measure length or volume.
Describe measuring time intervals with clocks and digital timers.
Find average small distances and short times by measuring multiples, including pendulum periods.
Distinguish scalar quantities, which have magnitude only, from vectors, which have magnitude and direction.
Identify distance, speed, time, mass, energy and temperature as scalars.
Identify force, weight, velocity, acceleration and gravitational field strength as vectors.

Calculate average speed as total distance divided by total time.
Sketch, plot and interpret distance–time and speed–time graphs.
Recognise increasing speed as acceleration and decreasing speed as deceleration.

Calculate speed from the gradient of a straight-line distance–time graph section.

State that near Earth free-fall acceleration is approximately constant at 9.8 m/s².

Explain centre of gravity and locate it in rectangular blocks, spheres and cylinders.

Describe how centre-of-gravity position affects the stability of simple objects.
State the kinetic, gravitational, chemical, elastic, nuclear, electrostatic and thermal energy stores.
Describe energy transfers between stores by mechanical work, electrical work, heating, and electromagnetic or sound waves.

Define power as work done or energy transferred per unit time and use both equations.

State that mass measures the quantity of matter in an object.

Describe particle arrangement, separation and motion in solids, liquids and gases, using simple diagrams.
Relate particle motion to temperature.
Recognise random particle motion in suspensions as evidence for the kinetic particle model.
Explain how particle forces, separations and motion determine solid, liquid and gas properties.

Explain gas pressure as force per area from particles colliding with surfaces.
Explain how temperature at constant volume and volume at constant temperature affect a fixed gas mass's pressure.

Describe condensation and freezing using particle ideas.

Explain conduction in solids through lattice vibrations and mobile electrons in metals.

Know that Earth's temperature depends on absorbed and emitted radiation.
Describe experiments comparing good and poor thermal radiation emitters.
Describe experiments comparing good and poor thermal radiation absorbers.
Identify and explain everyday applications and consequences of conduction, convection and radiation.
Describe states of matter using particle arrangement, separation, forces and motion; relate temperature and gas pressure to particle motion and collisions.
Explain thermal expansion and describe melting, boiling, evaporation, condensation and freezing, including factors affecting evaporation and associated temperature changes.
Describe and explain thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation, including their properties, applications and experimental investigation.
Know that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Describe wave motion using vibrating ropes, springs and water-wave experiments.
Explain transverse waves as vibrations perpendicular to propagation, including electromagnetic, water and seismic S-waves.
Explain longitudinal waves as vibrations parallel to propagation, including sound and seismic P-waves.
Describe wavelength, frequency, crest, trough, amplitude and wave speed.
Describe reflection, refraction and diffraction of waves.

Describe diffraction through a narrow gap.
Relate diffraction to wavelength and gap size.
Use ray diagrams to define the normal, incidence angle and reflection angle.

State and use equality of incidence and reflection angles.
Explain why a plane-mirror image is virtual.
Use diagrams, measurements and calculations for plane-mirror reflection.
Define refraction as a light ray's direction change between media.
Define and use the normal, incidence angle and refraction angle in ray diagrams.
Describe light passing through a transparent material at two-medium boundaries.

Use n = sin i / sin r.

Define the critical angle and explain total internal reflection above it.
Explain optical-fibre total internal reflection and give applications.
